Viewing this from a mechanical engineering and heat transfer student the fact that the 40 series can give the same performance for roughly half the electricity consumption means 2 major things:
1. Electricity bills. I don't know about you, if someone else pays your bills, but electricity is becoming more expensive day by day.
2. This also means, less energy being wasted as heat. Which results to your A/C working less to leep your room cool ,and the giant heatbox that is your pc. 
Imagine heat as capacity. Heat is energy. I'd much rather have most of the energy going into processing rather than into heat that my A/C will eventually have to get rid off. 
Now if you live in colder environments, go for anything else than 40 series 😂

text: Power consumption, heat and noise are big for me. I don't know if I speak for many PC gamers, but I tend to run discarded professional workstations as a platform for my gaming PC's. I can usually get them for free after they are a few generations old. These PC's while powerful and able to support discrete GPU's, they do not have tons of airflow and also their power supplies don't have the same wattage or PCIe cables as aftermarket gaming PCs do. For me, staying well below 200W for the GPU is a hard requirement. I am finally able to replace my 1070ti with something that is nearly twice as powerful while staying in (actually below) my existing card's 180W thermal envelope. The same cannot be said for the AMD cards or even the 4070 series.

No, I didn't appreciate your 4060 Ti review because the focus of the review seemed misguided. 

Is it great that it's very power efficient? Yes, but it's not a server product. 
Is it great that DLSS 3 can boost performance? Yes, but only for games that support it.
Is it great that it has RT cores? Yes, but why would you sacrifice performance at this price bracket?

text:
A bit behind on WAN show vods, but came back to take a look at this video after the first 5 minutes of last weeks WAN show, Unsure where the rest of the WAN show discussion goes, but I see both sides on this one. 

Sure you start out with the explicit sarcasm dunking on nvidia and the card, but then you go on to say "There is legitimately a fair bit to like about the RTX 4060 TI". To me, that sounds generally along the lines of, "its not a perfect card, but it is somewhat reasonable." You then talk through those points, and follow them up with "but you shouldn't pull the trigger without getting the full story." Yes this is indeed an explicit call to not buy it yet, but it feels(and kind of is) talking people back from the edge, basically telling them, you should be on the fence about this card, when realistically, while not complete trash, other more reasonable options exist. Yes I know this is meant to be a video for any future price, but I think its foolish to accidentally mislead current buyers(and future buyers for that matter, this issue so far is cost agnostic) so point out the benefits when the price drops who knows when in the future. And sure yes, the entire video as a collective, tells the whole story, but you know how important the first minute or so is, and I think the first minute(ish) sets the wrong expectations.

The first minute (up until the major tone shift) where you start dunking on the card's VRAM contains only (sarcastic) praise, and the good parts of the card. Nothing in a negative tone(No the sarcasm doesn't count because the whole sarcastic part is selling the negatives with a positive tone) and I think its way too easy to misunderstand the video just by having the wrong frame of mind, hence where these comments are coming from.

text:
4060Ti flops in the following categories: 

1. Price: at least $100 overpriced for the 8GB version, $150 - for the 16GB version.
2. Performance: now, this and the price are interconnected and form a price-performance, also known as FPS-per-dollar, balance, which is abysmal for 4060Ti. It would have been better off classed as 4050Ti instead. 
3. Memory: both in volume for 8Gb version and bus width in general. It is a strictly 1080p card, with additional texture settings limitation imposed by 8GB of memory. Also, the 32MB L3 cache is absolutely insufficient for higher resolutions. Remember RX 6900XT (256 bit bus) versus RTX3090 (384 bit bus and faster GDDR6X) reviews? At 1080p 6900XT was quite successfully headbutting with the oposition (until raytracing was switched on), while at 4K it was losing disproportionately - and it had 128MB of cache. 

The only win that is very arguable is power consumption, but that is even more proof that this card is just a glorified 4050Ti.

text:
I did catch a flaw in your review. Resizable BAR is NOT required for the GPU to use system memory. It's just that it will be even slower, since the GPU will essentially have to bankswitch, accessinly only X amount of system RAM at a time.  

I don't have Resizable BAR, but my computer lists 2GB of shared memory for my GPU. Windows will actually allow you to share up to 50% of your main memory. 

I also have seen at least some games that will reduce their memory requirements as much as they can under memory pressure. They can load in lower resolution textures, for example. It makes sense for a game to use more VRAM when available, even when it doesn't technically have to, just like how, say, Chrome will use more memory in a computer that has 16GB than one that has 8GB.

text:
Here's the most typical use case, though: Person has 1070 or 1060 or 1660 or RX 580 level of GPU and wants to upgrade to a NEW card (not used) that lets them continue playing all the games they want at 1080p. 4060 and 4060Ti fit the bill at their respective price points. You should NEVER be upgrading every generation from a 60 or 60ti to the next generation's version of it. Think about how lame going from a 2060 Super to a 3060Ti would be, performance wise. It's always like this.

Basically, saying "this isn't a big improvement over the past generation's equivalent card" is a weird take because at the 60, 60ti, and 70 level, it basically never is, it's always incremental. The big draw here is low power consumption, low price points, av1 encoding, dlss 2 and 3, productivity COMPATIBILITY, and ability to game just fine on mainstream (not weird half-assed console ports using 50% more VRAM than they should at launch) games.

text:
The only positive I see here is the power consumption. Otherwise, the card is cut down in every way: the GPU is tiny and underwhelming, VRAM capacity on the verge of serviceable (even at 1080p, in A Plague Tale: Requiem, it is completely unplayable (sub 20fps) at 1080p max and even a full preset lower it has big framedrops if you suddenly pan the camera), it has a narrow memory bus and very low bandwidth for a 60 class card, and the PCIe interface was cut down, which can have a measurable performance impact for someone on a PCIe gen 3 system (and that includes Intel up to the 10th gen, which are perfectly modern and capable chips - up to 8 cores and up to 5GHz are nothing to sneeze at).

I would also like to underline what I mentioned in passing: we have spotty performance at 1080p on a 60 series card on the day of its release!

As has been noted, Nvidia's pricing and nomenclature is completely disconnected from manufacturing costs (a small GPU is a cheap GPU, narrow memory bus means fewer PCB layers - cheap PCB, moderate power consumption - simple and cheap VRM solution and cooling...), so their pricing has nothing to do with "Moore's law being dead" and therefore requiring more resources (and money) to drive up the performance, because the die has shrunk, the price of manufacturing has gone down, meaning that Moore's law actually still somewhat alive, only the pricing seems to be immune to it.

text:
I only recently built my first PC, and I chose a 6700XT. My main motivation was the VRAM capacity, as I've never experienced ray-tracing, so I don't know what I'm missing. Given Nvidia's allergic reaction to 12GB of VRAM on mid-tier GPUs, I consider RTX to be a rich man's after-thought, or poor idiot's obsession. I've also never played a PC game that wasn't choppy on even medium settings (at least not since the 90's), and recent games have been the worst. So, at $340 I wasn't expecting a miracle GPU.

I was hoping to get to experience Cyberpunk on medium settings at 1080p. That's all I was expecting. Coming from 5-20 FPS on low settings at 720p (I actually played, finished, and enjoyed the game in that state lol), that would be a miracle to me.

What I got instead was completely maxed out settings at 1440p at around 60 FPS! The 6700XT eats everything I throw at it and never complains or skips a beat. I don't think I've experienced a single stutter, even though I'm waiting on the edge of my seat for JUST ONE to happen every time I play a game on it.

text:
That is part of it but nowhere near the whole truth. 
R9 290X in 2014 was the first 8GB card, so we've soon had 8GB cards for 10 years. In regards to NVIDIA it's also nothing new, they have always been stingy about VRAM, like that 3.5GB fast + 0.5 GB slow VRAM issue with GTX 970 which they got sued over. A lot of games are also developed based on the specifications of consoles that are current, plus maybe one or two higher presets for PC. The PS4 for example had shared RAM of 8GB's, the PS5 now has shared RAM of 16GB's with roughly 12GB maximum usable for VRAM purposes. This means developers can and will use that extra memory to create higher quality assets and thus requirements also raise on PC side.

text:
The 6750 XT is on Newegg right now, NEW, for as low as 330 USD (includes shipping, but this is also factoring in a $10 rebate card). It's a little bit faster than a 6700 XT, making its performance almost identical (on average) to a 4060 ti, except that it also has 12GB of Vram. The 6700 XT is also as low as 320 USD, and I also saw a very good quality model of 6700 XT (the Sapphire Pulse) for 345 USD (I'd recommend that over the other two). Deals in Canada aren't quite as good, but the 6700 XT and/or 6750 XT are still looking like the best options to me. I would try to stay away from any 8GB cards at this point when the 6700 XT is available for not that much more. The only other card which I think could also be quite good is the 16GB A770 from Intel, but just know that the software and drivers are likely to still be a little bit more rough around the edges. 

Trust me, the 6750 XT or 6700 XT for those prices is a much better deal, and is going to be a better deal than the 7600 as well most likely. 

On the other side, the 6800, 6800 XT, and even the 4070 all look like much better deals as well (the deal for the 4070 with a $100 steam gift card makes it pretty compelling, if you can still find that deal). These are all going to be much better alternatives to the 16GB 4060 ti. You can also look to Intel for some better value options, and the used market is also likely to have a lot of better options as well.

text:
There are a few things going on that I feel like helps no one.

1. Unrealistic expectations. A 4060Ti which is on-par with a 3060Ti but at 30% less power sounds great. The problem is how much more expensive it is. I don't think inflation alone explains the cost.
2. Shifting goal posts - wasn't the 3080 considered decent for 4k/60 gaming? Isn't the 4070 on par with that now? So what has changed? Just the new titles that are more demanding? how does the 4070 do against those titles from the era?
3. Release cadence. I know we like to compare to last gen, but I can't imagine that the average consumer is upgrading video cards every generation. I would they at most do every other one.

Don't get me wrong - I am not trying to make excuses here. These cards are very overpriced for their "tier" (naming convention) and inflation alone does not explain that increase. Still though, if you are in the 900/1000/2000 series, I would have to imagine even a 4060Ti would be a decent upgrade (depending on sku).

Still though nvidia needs to chill with these prices or they will end up driving more and more folks towards consoles. At this point, consistent decent performance/visuals across all titles on a PS5 is sounding very appealing. Especially when what was considered pretty good at $1500 will now cost you almost $3000.... and relative to a $500 PS5, neither sound great.

author: @grandrtiv26

text:
@dangerous8333  Not really. The pure grunt difference is quite solid, and the ray tracing is huge step up too, if you use it.

1440 max settings you were looking at about a 60% jump in framerates on most games (eg Horizon Zero Dawn, RE3) so hardly a "wasted" upgrade. Even on games with less of a boost (like Assassin's Creed Odyssey)  it's still good for a 30-40% jump, which is a solid generational jump from a 2080 or similar 2070 Super level. 

And then there's DLSS 2 which was a sizable improvement too, and helps on the vram issue by rendering at lower res.

And 2 GB more vram, which we can all admit wasn't enough but STILL places it above that 8gb vram wall the 4060ti and 3070TI are hitting. Plus, you have faster vram access as well on the 3080.

While a 12gb 3080 would have been much better than 10gb it wasn't a US$200 better card which is where they were priced when I was shopping. You were better off saving the $200 and putting it to your next upgrade.

But should I have bought the 6900XT for the same coin? Absolutely. Still regretting that.


Had I not been able to sell the 2070 Super for good coin, would I have done it? Nope. But as it turned out probably lucky that I did.

text:
To be fair, in generations prior, bus bandwidth was more important that buffer size for the simple reason that memory chips were just not very fast.  Now we have 21-24gbps chips and the on-die cache is massively improved. (although the on-die cache is actually slower than prior gen, it's 8x bigger)

Something else of note is that the more channels (bus width) you have, the more complex and layered the pcb must be.  So Nvidia isn't just saving on the gddr chips, it's saving on board complexity!

Its a 4050... It's clear they moved every card up a tier in naming only, and in some cases boosted the price on top of it. The 4070 is a 4060ti they are charging $600 for. This is a 4050 they want $400 for and the 16 GB 4050 will be $500. Been a rough 6 years... 

2000 series we just got ray tracing for the money....

4000 series Nvidia doing this slight of hand naming scheme while upping the prices even more

I don't hate these companies.... I'm a "fan" of Intel, AMD, and NVIDIA  but I'm not a "fan boy" for any of them. I have to say I'm hoping this bites them in the ass hard and they get stuck with a bunch of these cards and the prices tank. They could have cleared the 3000 series with large price reductions and still had solid margins. These 4000 series cards could be priced 20-30% lower and Nvidia would be doing amazing still... Yes the stock price wouldn't be $300,  ~10 times higher than it was not so long ago but would still be a fantastic company. As a tried and true capitalist I hope the market (we gamers) punish by not buying. I technically have the money to upgrade but I refuse to pay these garbage prices. 

I'm running a 2070 super, I wasn't all that excited about the purchase but my 970 sli rig turned into a single 970 when SLI died. My GPU is 4-5 year (?) old tech and I still have to pay 20% more again to get a worthwhile upgrade? Is it 5-6 years to get what would used to get every 2-3? Sad. Nvidia and ATI (AMD) used to give us a lot more value. The tech sector has done so well over the last 20 years because they gave the consumer so much value, more for your money (with some exceptions) every launch. 

Progress is slowing in terms of value to the consumer. Whether it's because margins and stock price rule the roost, or the companies are not good enough to deliver what we come to appreciate them for.... it's just sad to me either way. Seems as CPUs are not going up in terms of cost like GPUs, seems to me it's just a cash grab and a middle finger to all their loyal customers and fans.

I'll keep my wallet in my back pocket until they stop repaying my support as a customer with this much disrespect.

Here is how it goes:
The rtx 4060Ti is a 50 class card, marketed as a 60Ti class card sold for 70 class prices.
The rtx 4070 is a 50Ti class card, marketed as a 70 class card, sold at 80 class prices.
The rtx 4070Ti is a 60 class card, marketed as a 70Ti class card, sold at 90 class prices
The rtx 4080 is a 70 class card(389mm^2 vs rtx 3070 392mm^2), marketed as an 80 class card sold at insane prices
The rtx 4090 is an 80 class card, markted as a 90 class card, sold at ludicrous prices...

So here are how prices go:
4060 8GB - 220$
4060Ti 8GB - 270$
4070 - 350$
4070Ti - 420$
4080 - 600$
4090 - 900 -1000$

Anything more is unacceptable.

text:
I'm not entirely convinced by the "games require more than 8GB of VRAM" statement. Modern GPUs are designed such that the RAM will be filled up as far as possible to be more efficient and to add redundancy for better stability. This means that a GPU with a large VRAM capacity will fill it up far more than it actually needs, without a direct effect on performance. That means that a 12GB card could be using 10GB during game X, while an 8GB card uses 7GB without any performance hit. Basically the same as how adding more wheels to a car won't increase its top speed. 
The reduced memory bandwidth, however, does have an impact on performance, though Nvidia apparently covered that (partly) with more and faster cache.

text: @ever611  I write computing software that works with matrices that have effectively no upper limit on their size. As the matrices become larger, CPUs just can't keep up in terms of speed. It's the type of computing that makes sense for GPUs, and I want to target people with access to HPC facilities/supercomputers, which tend to predominantly support Nvidia (including the one I have access to). Since it's so heavily used, there's also just a ton of resources on CUDA programming. OpenCL or Vulkan compute could be viable, and I would love to eventually support non-proprietary alternatives to CUDA, but CUDA is going to be the lowest resistance route to reaching the most people I'm trying to target

We need AMD to do something...

text:
Game designer (in progress) here, on the note of the VRAM thing.

Pretty much it's just industry growing pains, developers are pushing the traditional geometry shading method to it's limit in regards to complexity and it's overwhelming VRAM busses (and CPUs) all around.

Tack on UE4 not being built for that level of complexity like in Jedi Survivor or Hogwarts Legacy, you get a lot of problems.

We know this is a growing pain thing because Fortnite with UE5 with Nanite enabled, the mode that HAS EVERY SINGLE BLADE OF GRASS BEING A MODEL runs actually pretty fine on VRAM despite the current size and complexity of the game map despite that vegetation change when Nanite is on resulting in a geometric complexity at least at the level of Jedi Survivor.

Virtualized Geometry/Mesh Shading is the solution to the VRAM problem as you only need to make your full-res model and a PLOD (Preferably), versus the Full-Res Model, 4-6 LOD tiers, then the Persistent LOD of standard shading/geometry. 

When models are AS Complex as they are nowadays, those extra LOD tiers are not "Simple" at all unless a developer bruteforce optimizes it which you only see on console Exclusives because PC players like extra scaling so you have to forego that to a degree or other consoles may not take kindly to the LOD Setup you have for that specific console.
